article.body_html:
Anyone reading local rental listings or chatting with a shop in Hanoi soon meets three short words: xe số, xe côn tay and xe ga. Together they tell you a lot about how a motorbike is ridden, and mixing them up is a common reason a visitor ends up on a bike that feels wrong.

The three words in one table

Vietnamese termPlain EnglishLeft hand and left footUsually suits
xe số (gear bike, often called semi-automatic)A small motorbike with a foot gear lever and no hand clutchHand holds the handlebar; foot changes gearRiders happy to shift gears but who do not want a clutch lever
xe côn tay (clutch bike)A motorbike with a hand clutch lever and a foot gear lever, often sportierHand pulls and releases the clutch; foot changes gearExperienced riders used to a manual clutch
xe ga or xe tay ga (scooter)An automatic scooter: no gear lever and no clutch leverHand usually works the rear brake lever; foot rests on the floorMost first-time visitors and anyone who wants the simplest controls

The word "côn" means clutch, and "tay" means hand, so xe côn tay is literally a hand-clutch bike. "Số" means gear or number. In everyday speech "ga" is the throttle, and a xe ga is the kind of bike where turning the throttle is all you do to go faster. Some people also use "xe số" loosely for any bike with gears, so a listing that says only "xe số" may not tell you whether there is a clutch lever.

What your hands and feet actually do

On a xe ga, both hands have brakes (usually the right hand for the front wheel and the left for the rear), the right hand twists the throttle, and your feet simply stand on the floor. There is nothing to shift.

On a xe số and a xe côn tay the rear brake is a foot pedal under your right foot, not a lever, which is easy to forget if you have only ridden scooters. On a xe số, the left foot works a gear lever beside the engine, tapping it to change gear, but the left hand has no clutch to manage, so the starting and stopping routine is simpler than on a manual motorcycle. On a xe côn tay, the left hand squeezes the clutch lever each time you change gear or stop, while the left foot shifts. Starting smoothly takes practice, and in stop-and-go traffic the clutch hand and the shifting foot are busy all the time.

Other words you will see on listings

Word or abbreviationMeaningWhy it matters
phân khối or "cc"Engine size, in cubic centimetresA bigger number usually means more power; 50cc and 110cc bikes feel very different from a 150cc sports bike
xe điệnElectric bike or scooterRange and charging matter; ask how the battery is handled
xe 50cc or xe 50 phân khốiA small-engine bike, often gentler and easier for a beginnerCheck what is on offer and ask about speed and load
đời xeModel yearAn older bike may be simpler but can feel more worn

Thuê xe máy Nguyễn Hà gives its reference prices in categories such as manual, automatic, electric and 50cc bikes, and for two named models, Vision and Air Blade. If you rent from it, ask whether its "manual" bikes have a hand clutch. These are reference prices only: confirm the bike and the rate before booking. The motorbike rental prices in Hanoi page lists them.

Which one should a visitor choose?

If you are unsure, a xe ga is the easiest place to start: with no clutch and no gears, you can concentrate on the traffic. Choose a xe số only if you are comfortable changing gear with your foot while riding in a crowd. Choose a xe côn tay only if you already ride a clutch bike regularly and can start, stop and hold a hill smoothly. If you have not ridden for a while, the guide to automatic versus semi-automatic in stop-start Hanoi traffic compares the controls in more detail.

Why English listings can mislead

English-language listings translate these words loosely. A clutchless xe số is often described as "semi-automatic", while a bike with a hand clutch may be called "manual" or just "gear bike", and both are sometimes shortened to "manual" in a quick message. A xe ga is usually called a scooter or an "automatic". Because the labels overlap, do not rely on one word: read the description, and ask whether the bike has a hand clutch lever and a foot gear lever. A good listing says plainly whether there is a hand clutch, how many gears the bike has and what size the engine is.

Clearing up a listing with three questions

If a listing is unclear, ask three things in writing before you pay: is it a xe số, a xe côn tay or a xe ga; does it have a hand clutch; and what size is the engine? If you want to ask in Vietnamese, these short lines work: "Xe này là xe số hay xe ga?" (Is this bike a gear bike or a scooter?) and "Xe có côn tay không?" (Does it have a hand clutch?). Keep the answers in the chat so that you can show them at pick-up.

A short message you can paste: "Hello, I would like to rent a xe ga (an automatic scooter) for these dates. I have not ridden a bike with a clutch. Which scooters do you have in that category, and what are the rates? Please confirm the bike and the rate before I book." It is polite, specific and leaves no doubt about the type of bike you want. A fuller message for any booking is in the guide to writing a motorbike rental booking message for Hanoi.

For more advice on getting started, read motorbike riding tips for first-time riders and browse the Manual & Semi-Automatic Motorbikes category.
